title: Class 5 Maths Tenths and Hundredths (NCERT Chapter 10) + Free Quiz
meta_title: Class 5 Maths Tenths and Hundredths Guide
meta_desc: Understand Class 5 maths tenths and hundredths with money and length examples, fraction-decimal conversion, a worked case study and a free 8-question quiz.
excerpt: Every time a shopkeeper hands back ₹2.50, your child is reading a decimal. Here is how NCERT Class 5 Chapter 10 turns tenths and hundredths into something they already know, plus a solved case study and a quick quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Hand a Class 5 child ₹18.75 and ask what the ‘.75’ means, and most will say ‘seventy-five paise’ without blinking. Ask them to write three-quarters of a rupee as a decimal on paper, though, and the confidence disappears. That gap is exactly what NCERT Class 5 maths tenths and hundredths (Chapter 10) sets out to close — it takes the decimals children already use with money and length every day and gives them the notation and the reasoning behind it.

The chapter is short but it carries a lot. Get tenths and hundredths right in Class 5 and decimal operations in Class 6 and 7 feel obvious. Rush it, and children spend years unsure where the decimal point goes. Here is how I teach it, section by section, with a solved case study at the end.

What a tenth and a hundredth actually are

Split one whole into 10 equal parts and each part is a tenth, written 0.1 or as the fraction 1/10. Split one whole into 100 equal parts and each is a hundredth, written 0.01 or 1/100. The first digit after the decimal point is the tenths place; the second is the hundredths place. So in 3.46, the 4 means four tenths and the 6 means six hundredths.

A ten-by-ten grid is the single best tool here. One full grid is 1 whole, one column (or row) is one tenth, one small square is one hundredth. Shade 37 small squares and a child can see, all at once, that 0.37 is the same as 37/100 and as three tenths plus seven hundredths.

Money is decimals in disguise

This is where the chapter feels effortless, because Indian children handle rupees and paise long before they meet a decimal point. One rupee is 100 paise, so paise are simply hundredths of a rupee.

  • ₹0.10 is 10 paise — one tenth of a rupee.
  • ₹0.05 is 5 paise — five hundredths of a rupee.
  • ₹7.25 is 7 rupees and 25 paise, or 7 whole and 25 hundredths.

The one mistake to watch for: writing 5 rupees 5 paise as ₹5.5. It is ₹5.05 — the paise always take two decimal places because there are 100 of them in a rupee. I make children read the two digits after the point as ‘paise’ every single time until it sticks.

Length: metres, centimetres and millimetres

Length works the same way, which is the quiet gift of the metric system. One metre is 100 centimetres, so a centimetre is one hundredth of a metre. One metre is 1000 millimetres.

So 1 m 45 cm is written 1.45 m, and 2 m 8 cm is 2.08 m (not 2.8 m — the same two-place trap as paise). Measuring a school desk or a cricket bat and writing the length both ways, in cm and in m, makes the conversion concrete instead of a rule to memorise.

Reading, writing and comparing

To compare two decimals, line up the decimal points and compare place by place, left to right — tenths first, then hundredths. A common wrong answer is that 0.45 is bigger than 0.5 ‘because 45 is bigger than 5’. It is not: 0.5 is five tenths, which is 0.50, and 50 hundredths beats 45 hundredths. Writing the missing zero (0.5 as 0.50) settles the argument instantly.

Seven hundredths7/1000.077 paise
Twenty-five hundredths25/1000.25₹0.25 (25 paise)
One and five tenths1 5/101.51 m 50 cm

Converting between fractions and decimals

Fractions with a denominator of 10 or 100 become decimals directly. 6/10 is 0.6; 43/100 is 0.43; 9/100 is 0.09. Going the other way, read the decimal aloud: 0.8 is ‘eight tenths’, so 8/10; 0.17 is ‘seventeen hundredths’, so 17/100.

The one that trips children up

A denominator of 10 gives one decimal place; a denominator of 100 gives two. So 3/10 is 0.3, but 3/100 is 0.03. The zero is doing real work — it holds the tenths place empty so the 3 lands in hundredths. This is worth ten minutes of deliberate practice on its own.

A worked case study: Meera’s stationery bill

NCERT loves putting decimals inside a real situation, so let me walk through one. Meera buys a notebook for ₹24.50, a pen for ₹12.75 and an eraser for ₹3.05. She pays with a ₹50 note.

How much did she spend? Line up the points and add: 24.50 + 12.75 + 3.05. The hundredths give 0 + 5 + 5 = 10, so write 0 and carry; the tenths give 5 + 7 + 0 + 1 = 13, and so on. The total is ₹40.30.

What change should she get? 50.00 − 40.30 = ₹9.70, which is 9 rupees and 70 paise. Notice how writing ₹50 as 50.00 keeps the places lined up — the same trick as adding a zero when comparing. That single habit prevents most decimal errors at this age.

This is the whole point of case-study questions: the maths is Class 5 tenths and hundredths, but the child has to read a situation, pick the operation, and keep the decimal point honest. It is closer to real life than a page of bare sums, and it is where marks are won or lost in exams.

quiz.title: Class 5 Tenths and Hundredths Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions on tenths, hundredths, money, length and fraction-decimal conversion. Choose an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: NCERT Class 5 Maths Chapter 10 Tenths and Hundredths

questions.q: How is 5 rupees and 5 paise written using the rupee symbol?
questions.explanation: Paise always take two decimal places, so 5 paise is 0.05. The amount is ₹5.05, not ₹5.5.

questions.q: What is 7/100 written as a decimal?
questions.explanation: A denominator of 100 means two decimal places. The 7 goes in the hundredths place, so 7/100 = 0.07.
Write 0.5 as 0.50. Fifty hundredths is greater than forty-five hundredths, so 0.5 is greater.

questions.q: How do you write 2 m 8 cm in metres?
questions.explanation: A centimetre is one hundredth of a metre, so it takes two places. 8 cm is 0.08 m, giving 2.08 m.

questions.q: What is 0.6 written as a fraction?
questions.explanation: 0.6 is read as six tenths, so it is 6/10.

questions.q: In the number 3.46, what does the digit 4 stand for?
questions.explanation: The first digit after the decimal point is the tenths place, so the 4 means four tenths.

questions.q: A ribbon is 0.75 m long. How many centimetres is that?
questions.explanation: 1 m is 100 cm, so 0.75 m is 75 hundredths of a metre, which is 75 cm.

questions.q: Ravi buys pencils for ₹12.50 and pays with a ₹20 note. What change does he get?
questions.explanation: Write ₹20 as 20.00 and subtract 12.50. The change is ₹7.50, or 7 rupees and 50 paise.

faq.q: What is the difference between a tenth and a hundredth?
faq.a: A tenth is one of 10 equal parts of a whole, written 0.1 or 1/10. A hundredth is one of 100 equal parts, written 0.01 or 1/100. In a decimal, the first digit after the point is tenths and the second is hundredths.

faq.q: Why is 5 paise written as ₹0.05 and not ₹0.5?
faq.a: There are 100 paise in a rupee, so paise are hundredths and always need two decimal places. ₹0.5 would mean 50 paise, while 5 paise is ₹0.05.

faq.q: How do you compare two decimals like 0.4 and 0.35?
faq.a: Line up the decimal points and add a zero so both have the same number of places: 0.40 and 0.35. Then compare, so 0.40 is greater than 0.35.

faq.q: How do I convert a fraction to a decimal in Class 5?
faq.a: If the denominator is 10, write one decimal place (3/10 = 0.3). If it is 100, write two places (43/100 = 0.43). Reading the decimal aloud reverses it: 0.09 is nine hundredths, so 9/100.
